What’s the hottest show right now?

Sisters Who Make Waves, the reality show in which female stars over 30 compete for a place in a girl group, is a strong contender for the top spot.

The hottest drama?

The one with Zhang Dongsheng, the teacher every schoolkid in China is now scared of (The Bad Kids), is easily in the top three.

The hottest song?

“Mojito” may be the only answer.

With this strongly Latin-flavored song, Jay Chou, the Mandopop superstar, has once again answered the question “Who is Jay Chou?”

## Wait, wasn’t today’s topic supposed to be timbre?

## Hang on, hang on~

I recently went to a concert devoted entirely to Jay Chou’s songs. The singer on stage worked his way from “Adorable Woman,” the first track on Jay’s first album, all the way to his recent hit “Mojito,” sharing his understanding of music and his admiration for Jay along the way:

“Listeners are entitled to their own tastes, but people who make music have to keep pushing forward, and Jay Chou is someone who pushed Chinese-language pop forward a little.”

“Jay Chou’s slow songs give his music its breadth, and his up-tempo songs give it depth. That’s how he pulled off the rare feat of being both musically serious and popular, so that professionals and ordinary listeners alike love him. In the process, he has quietly raised the public’s musical taste.”

At times it felt as if I’d wandered into a comedy show:

“When we were kids, parents told us: ‘Don’t copy Jay Chou, he mumbles so much nobody can understand him.’ Parents today: ‘Why can’t you be more like Jay Chou?!’”

Enough talk. Here’s the video:

Video source: http://whatmusicreallyis.com/

Singer: Ruihan Li (search for “李锐涵” on QQ Music or NetEase Cloud Music)

Having watched the video, did you notice that the microphone is placed rather far from the singer, as if it weren’t being used for amplification at all? Why abandon the mic? Because he felt the sound reinforcement system changed his timbre.

## At last, an awkward segue back to today’s topic…

## Couldn’t help it. That video was just too good not to work in somehow~

The chapter on sound in a middle-school physics textbook tells us that sound is produced by vibrating objects and can generally be described by three attributes: loudness, pitch and timbre.

Loudness: how strong or weak a sound seems to the ear. It is related to the amplitude of the vibration (the sound pressure): the larger the amplitude, the louder the sound.

Pitch: how high or low a sound seems to the ear. It is related to the frequency of the vibration: the higher the frequency, the higher the pitch and the brighter the sound; the lower the frequency, the lower the pitch and the deeper the sound.

So what is timbre, today’s topic? Timbre is the quality or character of a sound. The English word is timbre (careful: not timber!), and it is also called tone color or tone quality.

Let’s start with the definition given by the Acoustical Society of America (ASA): "that attribute of auditory sensation which enables a listener to judge that two nonidentical sounds, similarly presented and having the same loudness and pitch, are dissimilar"

Put simply: the attribute that lets us tell apart two sounds with the same loudness and pitch.

For example, when the same piece is played on a piano and on a violin, people can easily tell which is which, because the piano and the violin have different timbres. Likewise, with the same song, it’s easy to tell whether you’re hearing your idol’s original or some talented amateur’s cover, because the two singers have different timbres.

Look more closely at that definition, though, and it really is a lazy one. After reading it, you may still have only a hazy idea of timbre; it never says what timbre actually is. So much so that one researcher quipped that timbre is "...the psychoacoustician's multidimensional waste-basket category for everything that cannot be labeled pitch or loudness."

In other words: whatever in a sound isn’t pitch or loudness counts as timbre…

Psychoacousticians confess it’s tough: there are just too many other parameters to sort out, so they all got bundled together and called timbre…

Of the many physical parameters that affect timbre, the two most important are the frequency spectrum and the envelope.

What is a spectrum?

The figure above is the spectrum of a flute playing C4. The horizontal axis is frequency and the vertical axis is amplitude. The leftmost peak is the fundamental of C4, f0. Ideally, to produce a pure, precise C4, the spectrum would contain only this one peak. In reality, because of the flute’s construction and the particular way it produces sound, it can hardly produce a pure tone. In the spectrum, this shows up as further peaks to the right of the fundamental at f0: at 2f0 (the second peak from the left), 3f0 (the third peak from the left), and so on, at frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental. Together these peaks are called the harmonics of the fundamental, and it is precisely their positions, sizes and distribution that determine the timbre of different instruments playing the same note.

The next two figures show the spectra of a saxophone and a clarinet playing C4.

(Zhihu doesn’t support audio, so to hear the clarinet’s different timbres, head over to our WeChat Official Account.)

Listen on WeChat

As you can see, although the note is the same, the sizes and distribution of the harmonics in the spectra differ, and it is precisely these differences that let us hear which instrument is playing.

The video below shows the audio and the corresponding time-varying spectrum (spectrogram) of different instruments playing the same note, B2. In order, they are: piano, harpsichord, classical guitar, Indian sitar, viola, cello, baritone saxophone, bassoon, Japanese shakuhachi and accordion. Watch it to get a feel for the relationship between timbre and spectrum (the harmonics).

Video source: http://whatmusicreallyis.com/

Timbre is closely tied to the spectrum, that is, to the harmonics. So if we somehow change the harmonics of a given instrument, does that mean its timbre can change too?

It does.

Blow a flute with different force, for example, and the same note will sound a little different.

The three figures below show the spectrum of a flute playing C4 very softly, moderately softly and loudly. You can see how the harmonics differ, and each figure is followed by the matching audio, so click to hear the difference.

The talented voice actors online who play several characters at once rely on much the same principle.

What I described in an earlier answer is, in fact, also the result of our timbre being changed:

Why does my voice sound unfamiliar when I listen to a recording of myself? Is the recording what other people actually hear?

Besides the spectrum, another very important parameter is the envelope.

What is an envelope?

The red line in the figure below is the envelope of a sound signal. The horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is amplitude; the envelope describes how the sound changes over time.

The most common envelope model is ADSR, whose four letters are the initials of the model’s four main parameters: Attack, Decay, Sustain and Release.

Attack: the time it takes for the sound to rise from its onset to its maximum level.

Decay: the time it takes for the sound to fall from its maximum level to the sustain level.

Sustain: the level at which the sound holds after the decay.

Release: the time it takes, once the sustain ends, for the sound to fall from the sustain level to zero.

Change these four parameters and the same note will sound different. In the second video, the corresponding envelope is shown along the bottom.

So far we have covered two features that determine timbre, the spectrum and the envelope: one in the frequency domain, the other in the time domain. Understanding and studying timbre is really a matter of finding more features and sub-features. The sounds of the world are endlessly varied, and pinning down the core (sub-)features is not easy; artificial intelligence, today’s hot topic, is being put to work on the problem too. In 2018, researchers published a paper in Nature on how quickly humans recognize all kinds of timbres [1], which only goes to show that artificial intelligence still has a long way to go before it matches human intelligence.

References

1 Piazza, E.A., Theunissen, F.E., Wessel, D. et al. Rapid Adaptation to the Timbre of Natural Sounds. Sci Rep 8, 13826 (2018).

2 https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/music/
